title: Have you been to Tainan?
goal: Talk about experiences with 過 — and master a form typical of Taiwan that mainland textbooks call a mistake: 有 + verb.
bekal: tell 過 (have ever) apart from 了 (have done)
use the 有 + verb form heard all over Taiwan
talk about places in Taiwan and travel experiences

dialogs.title: 對話 — 週末去哪裡
dialogs.intro: With a long weekend coming up, the three of them talk about a trip outside Taipei.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Budi, have you ever been to Tainan?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: No. I've only been to Taipei and Keelung.
lines.literal: not — have. I — only — go-(ever) — Taipei — and — Keelung.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [那|Nà][你|nǐ][一定|yídìng][要|yào][去|qù]！[台南|Táinán][是|shì][我|wǒ][的|de][家鄉|jiāxiāng]。
lines.id: Then you have to go! Tainan is my hometown.
lines.literal: then — you — surely — must — go! Tainan — is — I — 's — home-village.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: What's fun to do in Tainan?

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.id: Lots of historic sites, and even more street food!
lines.literal: ancient-trace — very — many, small-eat — even — more!

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][有|yǒu][去過|qùguò][三次|sān cì]。[真的|Zhēn de][很|hěn][好吃|hǎochī]！
lines.id: I've been there three times. The food is seriously good!
lines.literal: I — have — go-(ever) — three — times. real — (one) — very — tasty!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Have you ever had danzai noodles?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [有|Yǒu][啊|a]！[還有|Hái yǒu][牛肉湯|niúròu tāng]，[早上|zǎoshang][喝|hē][的|de]。
lines.id: Sure have! And beef soup too, the kind you have in the morning.
lines.literal: have — (softener)! also — have — beef-meat — soup, morning — drink — (one).

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Beef soup for breakfast? How unusual!

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [台南|Táinán][人|rén][都|dōu][這樣|zhèyàng]。[你|Nǐ][沒|méi][吃過|chīguò][就|jiù][不算|bú suàn][來過|láiguò]。
lines.id: All Tainan people do that. If you haven't tried it, your visit doesn't count.
lines.literal: Tainan — person — all — this-way. you — not — eat-(ever) — then — not — count — come-(ever).

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: OK! So when do we go?
lines.literal: good! then — we — what — time — go?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [下個月|Xià ge yuè][有|yǒu][三天|sān tiān][連假|liánjià]。
lines.id: Next month there's a three-day long weekend.
lines.literal: below — (measure word) — month — have — three — day — joined-holiday.

lines.speaker: 阿明:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][爸媽|bàmā][家|jiā][可以|kěyǐ][住|zhù]。[不用|Bú yòng][錢|qián]！
lines.id: We can stay at my parents' place. Free!
lines.literal: I — dad-mom — home — can — stay. not — need — money!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [太|Tài][不好意思|bù hǎoyìsi][了|le]…[可是|Kěshì][謝謝|xièxie]！
lines.id: That's too kind of you… but thank you!

notes: ⚠️ **有去過 is a very Taiwanese form.** Grammar books from the mainland call it a mistake — they say 去過 alone is enough. But in Taiwan, 有 + verb is the normal form, heard everywhere, and it comes from the influence of Hokkien. Use it; you'll sound local.
**小吃 ("small eats") means street food or food-stall dishes**, not light snacks. Tainan is Taiwan's 小吃 capital, and people really do cross the island just to eat there.
**不算 means "doesn't count"** — an expression often used jokingly: *沒吃過就不算來過* ("if you haven't eaten it, your visit doesn't count").
⚠️ **太不好意思了 means "that's too kind, I feel bad"**, not "too embarrassing". It's the polite way to accept someone's kindness, and turning it down once before accepting is part of Taiwanese politeness.
**連假 ("joined holiday") is a long weekend** when a public holiday falls next to a weekend. All of Taiwan is on the move during 連假; book train tickets well in advance.

grammars.title: 過: have ever, at some point in your life
body: **過** is attached after a verb to say that you have **ever** experienced it — when doesn't matter. It talks about experience, not about one specific event.

head: Sentence
Pīnyīn
Meaning
rows: Have you ever eaten stinky tofu?

after: ⚠️ **The difference between 過 and 了 matters and is often mixed up.** *我去了台南* means "I went to Tainan" — a specific event, maybe just yesterday, maybe I'm still there. *我去過台南* means "I've been to Tainan" — an experience; I'm back now.
**過 is negated with 沒, and 過 STAYS**: *我沒去過* ✓. Compare 了, which disappears when negated: *我沒去* ✓, *我沒去了* ✗. Two markers, two behaviors.
**Frequency is counted with 次 (*cì*, time)**, placed **after** the verb: *我去過三次* — not *我三次去過*.

grammars.title: ⚠️ 有 + verb: the Taiwanese form missing from mainland textbooks
body: In Taiwan, 有 is often placed before a verb to stress that something **really did happen**. This form comes from Hokkien, and it's everywhere in everyday conversation.

head: Taiwanese form
Mainland textbook form
Meaning
rows: Did you see it or not?

after: **Why this is useful for you:** the 有 + verb form is much easier to use than 了, because it's negated with 沒有 without dropping anything, and you ask with 有沒有 without worrying about where 了 goes.
⚠️ **Don't use it in the formal grammar section of the TOCFL exam**, since the answer key usually follows the written standard. In conversation, it's correct and natural.
**This form is also a way to insist** when someone doubts you: *我有說啊！* ("I did say so!") It sounds slightly defensive, and you'll hear it a lot.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the pattern in the names: **台北 (Taiwan-north), 台中 (Taiwan-central), 台南 (Taiwan-south), 台東 (Taiwan-east)**. Four cities, four compass points — once you see the pattern, you'll never mix them up again. The ones that don't follow it are 高雄 and 花蓮.

blocks.title: Taiwanese street food you'll be asked about
items: **臭豆腐** *chòudòufǔ* — fried stinky tofu. ⚠️ This is the test of courage offered to every foreigner.
**擔仔麵** *dànzǎi miàn* — small Tainan noodle bowl with minced pork and shrimp.
**滷味** *lǔwèi* — assorted ingredients simmered in soy broth, picked yourself.
**鹽酥雞** *yánsūjī* — popcorn chicken fried with basil leaves.
**豆花** *dòuhuā* — sweet tofu pudding with peanuts and ginger syrup.
**芒果冰** *mángguǒ bīng* — mango shaved ice, a must in summer.

sections.title: Counting events: 次, 遍, 天

head: Word
Pīnyīn
Used for
Example
rows: how many times from start to finish

blocks.text: ⚠️ **All event counters stand AFTER the verb**, the opposite of time expressions, which stand before it. Compare: *我明天去* (time → before) but *我去過三次* (amount → after). If there's an object, the count still goes before the object: *我看了兩遍這本書* or *我這本書看了兩遍*.
